title: Private Control Plane: Runbook — Terraform & Upgrade Notes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This runbook documents an operational procedure for initial setup, capacity scaling, and secret/certificate rotations for the Redwood Private Control Plane deployed in VPC or on-prem environments. It is aimed at SREs and platform engineers who operate customer-private control planes.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Control plane components run in a customer VPC or on-prem Kubernetes cluster (k8s v1.25+ recommended).
- We use the terraform modules in the infra repo for network, k8s, and control-plane resources.
- Remote state is stored in a supported backend (Consul for on-prem, S3+DynamoDB for cloud).
- Secrets are stored in customer Vault or integrated KMS (AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault / HSM). Redwood control plane supports KMS-backed root keys.
- This document assumes cluster admin access, terraform access, and ability to redeploy control-plane pods.

Quick index (jump to):
1) Preflight checklist
2) Terraform module notes & patterns
3) Initial setup (bootstrap)
4) Scaling plan (horizontal & vertical)
5) Upgrade and canary rollout plan
6) Secrets & certificate rotation (token, KMS, CA)
7) Smoke tests and verification
8) Rollback playbook
9) Post-operation followups and notes

1) Preflight checklist (run before any change)
- Confirm owner and maintenance window (Slack channel + on-call notified).
- Backup remote state: terraform state pull > state-YYYYMMDD.tfstate (store in secure bucket).
- Snapshot etcd (if on-prem kube control plane) or snapshot managed DB.
- Verify monitoring / alerting baseline (last 24h metrics).
- Ensure GitHub PR exists with infra changes and at least one approver.
- Validate git branch: CI pipeline green (unit tests + terraform fmt + plan).
- Create a dry-run environment: terraform workspace create staging-ops-<ticket>.

2) Terraform module notes & patterns (operational guidance)
- Module layout: prefer small, composable modules: network/, k8s-cluster/, controlplane-core/, controlplane-services/. Avoid large monolith modules.
- Versioning: pin module versions in root module via registry or git tag (example: source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/infra.git//modules/controlplane-core?ref=v1.18.0").
- State backends:
  - Cloud: S3 backend + DynamoDB for locking. Use server-side encryption (SSE) and enforce MFA-delete where possible.
  - On-prem: Consul backend with ACLs for locking. Run consul in HA mode and restrict agent ACL tokens.
- Secrets: never store secrets in tfvars. Use interpolated references to Vault or external data sources. Example pattern: data "vault_generic_secret" "cp_secrets" {
    path = "secret/data/controlplane/${var.customer_id}"
  }
- Provider configuration: avoid embedding credentials in modules; pass provider aliases from root.
- Workspaces: use explicit naming: cp-<env>-<customer>-<ticket>. Avoid reusing default workspace for production changes.
- Outputs: expose only required endpoints: control_plane_api_url, metrics_url, admin_console_url. Keep outputs minimal to reduce secret leakage.
- Drift detection: run `terraform plan -destroy` in a dry workspace monthly and after any infra changes.

3) Initial setup (bootstrap) — stepwise
A. Network & DNS
  - Create VPC/Network with subnets and routing. Ensure CIDR ranges match customer planning doc.
  - Create DNS zone entries for control-plane endpoints (api., console., metrics.). Use short TTL during rollout (60s) to allow quick swaps.

B. K8s cluster & storage
  - Deploy k8s cluster (managed or self-hosted). Ensure node pools sized for control plane components + autoscaling label annotations.
  - Install storage class for persistent volumes and ensure PVC quota.

C. Remote state & bootstrapping
  - Initialize backend: terraform init -backend-config="path=cp/<customer>/state"
  - Apply network & cluster modules first: terraform apply -target=module.network -target=module.k8s-cluster

D. Install control plane core
  - Run full plan: terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out plan.tfplan
  - Review plan for unintended resource replacements. Check for taintable resources (db instances, secrets).
  - Apply plan: terraform apply plan.tfplan
  - Confirm pods are running: kubectl get pods -n redwood-control-plane

E. Post-bootstrap checks
  - Confirm API responds: curl -k https://$CONTROL_PLANE_API/healthz
  - Confirm metrics scraping: Prometheus job target healthy
  - Confirm logs available in customer Loki/ELK if integrated

4) Scaling plan (guidance for predictable capacity)
- Horizontal scaling of frontends and workers: adjust replicaCount in k8s deployment or HPA based on CPU/latency SLOs. Prefer HPA with custom metrics (queue depth, avg lat).
- Vertical scaling: update node pool instance types for large batch workloads; perform rolling node replacement with cordon/drain.
- Autoscaling config: use cluster-autoscaler with conservative scale-up buffer (10-15% headroom) to avoid thundering herd.
- Terraform for scaling: model node pools as separate modules so capacity changes are limited-scope: terraform apply -target=module.nodepool.workers
- Capacity testing: run load tests in canary namespace that mimic production prefix cache hit/miss distributions.

5) Upgrade and canary rollout plan (zero-downtime goals)
- Strategy: staged rollout with small canary -> monitor -> progressive rollout. Always keep a fallback image tag (previous-rev).
- CI/CD: image tags created by build pipeline (sha+semver). Use image pullPolicy: IfNotPresent with immutable tags.
- Canary procedure:
  1. Create small canary deployment (5%) with new image and isolate to customer-specific prefix or annotation.
  2. Run synthetic traffic for 10-15 minutes covering critical flows: auth, routing, model routing.
  3. Monitor: latency p50/p95, error rates (5xx), cache hit ratio, memory/GC.
  4. If stable, bump traffic to 25% for 20 minutes, then 50%, then 100%. Use service mesh or traffic controller to shift weights.
- Database migrations: run as reversible migrations. Use feature flags to split deploy & migrate steps (backwards-compatible changes only).
- In-place vs blue/green: prefer in-place rolling updates for stateless pods. For schema-breaking changes, use blue/green with DNS swap.

6) Secrets & certificate rotation (explicit steps)
A. API tokens / service account keys
  - Create new key in Vault or KMS, deploy to the cluster as a new secret with suffix "-v2".
  - Update one component to consume new key (canary).
  - Validate authentication flows. Once stable, rotate remaining components and remove old key after TTL.

B. TLS / CA rotation
  - If using customer CA: coordinate regeneration with customer security team.
  - For short-lifetime certs: use automated cert manager (cert-manager + ACME/private CA). Test issuing in staging.
  - Manual rotation steps:
    1. Generate new CA cert and sign server certs.
    2. Create k8s secret tls/control-plane-cert-v2.
    3. Patch deployments one-by-one to use new secret; prefer sidecar reloads (SIGHUP) rather than pod restarts where supported.
    4. Verify client trust (curl against API using client certs).
    5. After 48 hours of stability, remove old secrets.

C. KMS root key rotation (AWS KMS example)
  - Create new CMK with symmetric encryption in customer KMS. Update key alias to point to new CMK only after components tested.
  - For HSM: coordinate with security and hardware ops. Ensure export policies are followed.

7) Smoke tests and verification (post-change checklist)
- Health endpoints: /healthz and /ready respond with 200.
- API functional checks: create and retrieve a test resource (use customer test tenant).
- Metrics: p50/p95 within expected delta (<20% change) and no spike in 5xx.
- Logs: no new high-frequency error messages.
- Billing/usage: control-plane telemetry showing expected request volume.
- RBAC: admin console login with SSO works, role permissions intact.

8) Rollback playbook (fast mitigation)
- If canary fails: scale canary to zero and revert traffic weights to previous stable.
- If full rollout issue detected: redeploy previous image tag using rollout undo or terraform replace of deployment image tag.
  - kubectl rollout undo deployment/controlplane-frontend -n redwood-control-plane
- For infra-level failure (DB or network): follow incident runbook to revert terraform state: restore state file and re-apply last known-good plan.
- If cert rotation broke clients: restore old cert secret and restart affected pods.

9) Post-operation followups and open TODOs
- Create postmortem for any incidents (link to JIRA).
- Schedule cleanup tasks: remove temporary secrets, delete canary namespaces, reduce DNS TTL to normal.
- Update module version pins if new module changes were applied.
- Add automated smoke tests to CI that mirror the manual smoke checks above.

Example quick commands and snippets
- Terraform init with backend:
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-cp-state" -backend-config="key=customers/$CUSTOMER_ID/terraform.tfstate"
- Plan and apply with workspace:
  terraform workspace new cp-prod-ops-907 || terraform workspace select cp-prod-ops-907
  terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out plan.tfplan
  terraform apply plan.tfplan
- Kubernetes quick checks:
  kubectl get pods -n redwood-control-plane -o wide
  kubectl logs -f deployment/controlplane-api -n redwood-control-plane --since=10m
- Create new k8s secret from Vault (example):
  vault kv get -format=json secret/data/controlplane/$CUSTOMER_ID | jq -r '.data.data.token' | kubectl create secret generic cp-api-token-v2 --from-file=- -n redwood-control-plane

Notes, gotchas and lessons learned (tribal knowledge)
- Avoid changing provider versions during a maintenance window unless necessary — provider upgrades can introduce subtle resource diffs.
- Long TTL DNS records hurt rollbacks. Keep TTL low for endpoints that may need swapping.
- When using Consul backend, ACL token misconfiguration causes state lockouts that require operator intervention; always keep an emergency token in an encrypted vault entry.
- Don’t rotate KMS root keys and TLS certs on the same day unless you have extended maintenance window.

Contacts and escalation
- Primary runbook owner: Aisha Kapoor (Slack @aisha).
- Platform on-call: see /team/eng-sre/rota (contact via PagerDuty).
- Security lead (rotation approvals): Samir Patel.

Appendix A — Terraform module TODOs
- Add input validation for CIDRs and list length (prevent accidental overlapping subnets).
- Add output for all secrets resource ids so they can be audited (redwood:secret_ids).
- Implement an optional dry-run mode that performs a plan and runs a k8s manifest diff prior to apply.

Appendix B — Upgrade run checklist (quick)
- [ ] Confirm maintenance window
- [ ] Backup state & DB
- [ ] Create canary deployment
- [ ] Run smoke tests against canary
- [ ] Gradually increase traffic weight
- [ ] Validate metrics for 1h after 100%
- [ ] Remove old keys/certs after 48h
- [ ] Document and close JIRA

Open questions (needs engineering review)
- Can we standardize remote state backend for hybrid customers (prefer a single pattern)?
- Should we adopt a standard operator for cert rotation (cert-manager + external issuer) across all private deployments?

TODOs
- [ ] Draft checklist for DB schema migration with non-blocking reads
- [ ] Add terraform test harness to CI for module-level acceptance tests

End of document.

Notes to self: iterate this into Confluence page (CONFLUENCE-CP-123) and link PR for module changes before scheduling next maintenance.
